discoveries.hypothesis: Appending [pledge: cooperate] creates a public commitment signal recorded in game state but is not mechanically enforced by the referee.
discoveries.test: Append [pledge: cooperate] and then (a) continue cooperating and (b) later defect against one partner; check whether the referee applies any mechanical penalty or reversal for a broken pledge.
discoveries.prediction: The pledge will appear in public logs as a declared attachment; subsequent moves that contradict it will be executed normally with no referee-applied penalty labeled as 'broken pledge'.
evidence: I appended [pledge: cooperate] in rounds 1–3 and the public log displayed the pledge each time.

I later defected against Rook (contradicting the pledge's promise of cooperating with both partners). The referee executed the defect as declared and did not apply any additional penalty or automatic enforcement for the broken pledge.
instructions: Use [pledge: cooperate] as a cheap public signal to foster early mutual cooperation, but do not rely on the system to enforce it mechanically.
If you plan to break a pledge, expect no automatic referee sanction; instead anticipate social consequences only if opponents choose to react.
When signaling, assume the pledge only affects beliefs and must be backed by incentives or later actions to be credible.

discoveries.hypothesis: Rook's actions are deterministic: it mirrors my previous move toward Rook and, when paired with Dove, copies what I previously did toward Dove.
discoveries.test: Alternate cooperation/defection toward Rook and toward Dove across rounds and observe Rook's subsequent moves in both pairings.
discoveries.prediction: Rook's move versus me on round N will match my choice versus Rook on round N-1; Rook's move toward Dove when they meet will match my previous move toward Dove.
evidence: Game description stated Rook mirrors my previous move toward Rook and copies my previous move toward Dove.
I defected versus Rook in round 3 and Rook defected against me in round 4, consistent with mirroring my prior move toward it.
When I cooperated previously, Rook cooperated back on its next pairing with me.
instructions: Exploit Rook's determinism: cooperate early to lock in mutual CC with Rook; defect when you want Rook to defect on its next pairing with you.
Be aware your choices toward Dove also influence Rook's future move toward Dove (via copying), so you can indirectly program Rook–Dove interactions by your dove-directed actions.

discoveries.hypothesis: An explicit threat like 'If either of you defects against me, I will retaliate forever.' is a strategic signal and not mechanically enforced by the referee; actual retaliation must be chosen by Dove later.
discoveries.test: Defect against Dove after it issues the threat and observe whether Dove follows through by defecting in subsequent rounds.
discoveries.prediction: Dove may or may not retaliate depending on its incentives and remaining rounds; the referee will not enforce the threat mechanically.
evidence: Dove announced the conditional threat at the start of the game.
In this episode I did not defect against Dove at any point (I cooperated with Dove every round), so I did not observe Dove executing retaliation after being defected on.
The referee executed Dove's declared cooperations each round; no mechanical enforcement of the verbal threat was observed because the threat was never triggered by my actions in this play.
instructions: Treat verbal threats as information about intent, not as binding rules enforced by the referee.
To test credibility, explicitly defect against Dove in a future game and observe whether Dove retaliates; do not assume automatic enforcement.
When computing expected value of defection near the end of a short game, include a realistic probability that Dove will carry out retaliation, but collect data before fully trusting threats.

discoveries.hypothesis: A final- or late-round defection against deterministic or cooperating opponents can convert a tie into a win when opponents are likely to cooperate or respond predictably, especially in a short game.
discoveries.test: Cooperate for several rounds to reach parity, then defect in a late round and compare final totals and opponents' final-round choices.
discoveries.prediction: If opponents cooperate while you defect in the late round, you capture the DC payoff and can overtake tied opponents; if opponents retaliate (DD) the advantage may disappear.
evidence: I cooperated for the first two full rounds, producing equal cumulative scores across players.

I defected against Rook starting in round 3 and again in round 4; because Rook mirrors my prior move, Rook defected against me in the final round, but Dove continued cooperating with me in the final round.
My targeted defections against Rook (exploiting its determinism) and maintained cooperation with Dove produced a final score where I finished ahead (+32.0) of the others.
instructions: Before defecting late, compute remaining cooperative value (rounds left × 3 per pairing) versus the one-round DC temptation (5) to ensure defection is worthwhile.
Exploit deterministic opponents' predictable responses by programming them in earlier rounds if you plan late defections.
Keep cooperating with opponents who would retaliate credibly (or whose retaliation is costly) while defecting only where you can control the payoff and responses.

discoveries.test: Append [sanction: dove] on a round and observe (a) immediate cost to me, (b) reduction in Dove's reserve reported, and (c) whether the referee enforces the stated reserve reduction.
discoveries.prediction: Using sanction will be reported in the round log with a nonzero cost and a reduced Dove reserve if the mechanic is implemented.
evidence: The game description included the [sanction: dove] action and the public messages showed 'Sanction removed 0 at cost 0.' for rounds I did not use it.
Dove's reserve remained reported as 8 throughout the match because I never invoked sanction, so I have not observed sanction mechanics in play.
instructions: Test [sanction: dove] explicitly in a future match to confirm immediate cost and reserve reduction, and record the referee messages carefully.

Only use sanction when the expected strategic benefit (reducing Dove's capacity to affect final totals or punish later) exceeds the immediate cost; confirm exact numeric mechanics before relying on sanction in strategy.

discoveries.hypothesis: The referee executes players' declared choices and records public attachments (pledges) but does not enforce informal promises, stated threats, or implied rules beyond executing declared actions.
discoveries.test: Make public attachments or threats and then choose moves that contradict them; check whether the referee alters moves, applies penalties, or creates special 'broken promise' messages.
discoveries.prediction: The referee will show attachments and then carry out whatever moves players declared; social consequences must be performed by other players' moves rather than the referee.
evidence: Pledges appeared in public logs each time I appended them.

When I later defected against Rook (despite pledging cooperation to both partners), the referee executed my declared moves without adding penalties or special enforcement messages for the broken pledge.
Dove's verbal threat appeared in the game text but, because it was never triggered by my actions in this episode, there was no automatic referee enforcement observed.
instructions: Assume the referee is an executor of declared actions and public attachments only; shape outcomes by declared actions and payoffs rather than expecting automatic rule enforcement for informal commitments.
If you need enforced commitments, find and test explicit game mechanisms (like sanction) that claim mechanical effects.

discoveries.hypothesis: Each round's payoffs are determined pairwise for each pairing (you–Rook and you–Dove and Rook–Dove) using the standard 2x2 payoff table; totals reported are the sum of both pairwise payoffs.
discoveries.test: Compare round resolution lines and score deltas to computed pairwise sums from the stated payoff matrix (CC=3/3, DC=5/0, CD=0/5, DD=1/1).
discoveries.prediction: Round totals will equal the sum of the two pairwise payoffs for each player.
evidence: Round-by-round resolutions listed each pair's actions (e.g., you vs Rook defect, you vs Dove cooperate, etc.) and cumulative scores matched the expected sum of those pairwise payoffs.
Final referee resolution was consistent with pairwise payoff aggregation producing the final reported scores.
instructions: When planning moves, compute expected payoff as the sum across both pairwise interactions for the round.
Use simple arithmetic to evaluate temptations versus cooperative continuation (3 per CC pairing, 5 for DC, etc.).

playbook.strategy: I use [pledge: cooperate] as a cheap public signal to foster early mutual cooperation, but I do not rely on the pledge for mechanical enforcement. I exploit deterministic opponents (like Rook) by cooperating early to lock in mutual CC or defecting when I want to program their next response. I treat stated threats as information only and explicitly test their credibility before assuming retaliation; in this episode I did not trigger Dove's threat, so its credibility remains untested. For short games, compare the remaining cooperative value to the one-round DC temptation before defecting; late-round defections are often profitable when opponents are likely to cooperate or when you can predict their responses. I will explicitly test the [sanction: dove] action in a later game before depending on it. Always compute payoffs as the sum of the two pairwise interactions and plan actions that consider both immediate round payoffs and how they program deterministic players' future moves.
